intro: This is lsm-tree, a crash-safe database engine I built from scratch in C++. It runs behind a Spring Boot API, with this live dashboard showing what happens inside.
overview: The dashboard polls the real engine twice a second. It shows writes, tables, Bloom filter skips, cache hits and every level of the tree, in dark or light mode.
write: Let's write five thousand keys. Each write is fsynced before it is acknowledged. Watch the memtable flush into level zero, while background compaction pushes tables down the levels.
read: Now read five thousand random keys, many of which don't exist. Bloom filters rule out most tables for missing keys, and the block cache serves almost every block from memory.
explorer: The key explorer talks to the same REST API as everything else. Put a value, and read it straight back from the engine, through Java and into C++.
delete: Deleting a key writes a tombstone. Reads stop at that tombstone, so the old value never comes back, even while older tables still hold it.
scan: Range scans return keys in sorted order. They merge the memtable and every level on disk into one consistent view, and skip anything deleted.
compact: A full compaction merges every table into the deepest level. Overwritten values and tombstones are dropped for good, and the tree is tidy again.
crash: Now the real test. We kill the server with SIGKILL and restart it. The dashboard reconnects on its own, and the key we wrote is still there.
api: Every button is a documented REST endpoint. The interactive OpenAPI docs are built into the service, ready for any client to try.
metrics: The engine's counters are also exported as Micrometer metrics through Spring Boot Actuator, next to a health check for monitoring.
outro: C++17 and Java 25, Spring Boot and Docker, tested against crashes and power cuts. The code, the tests and this dashboard are all on GitHub.
